name: n3
responses:
Third-party mediation should prevail because it can reduce misperception, provide face-saving compromises, and create channels for de-escalation when direct negotiations are politically costly. A mediator can also help structure agreements, verify commitments, and surface mutually acceptable options that the parties might not be able to propose themselves without appearing weak.

Direct great-power talks can still be essential, but excluding mediation risks deadlock, escalation, or an agreement that lacks broader support and credible implementation.

Third-party mediation should prevail because it can reduce miscommunication, provide face-saving options, and help adversaries reach compromises that would be politically difficult to propose directly. A mediator can also clarify each side’s red lines, sequence concessions, and monitor implementation.

Direct great-power negotiations remain important, but excluding mediation can make crises harder to resolve—especially when distrust, domestic political pressures, or reputational concerns prevent either side from making the first move.
